description: Believing `let x = 'a'` is inferred as the literal type 'a', rather than widened to string.
Believing `const x = 'a'` is inferred as string, rather than the literal type 'a'.
Believing the properties of `const o = { k: 'a' }` keep the literal type 'a', rather than widening to string.
Believing `const xs = []` under strict mode is inferred as a fixed element type, rather than evolving as elements are pushed.
Believing a type annotation changes the value at runtime, such as converting or validating it.
Believing `x as number` converts the value to a number at runtime, rather than only telling the compiler to trust the type.
Believing the non-null assertion `x!` checks or removes null at runtime.
Believing any property of any union member can be read without narrowing.
Believing a value of type A | B exposes the members of both A and B, rather than only the members they share.
Believing `typeof x === 'object'` narrows out null.
Believing the `in` operator narrows by property value rather than by property presence.
Believing narrowing of a mutable variable persists inside a callback created after the check.
Believing a union narrows on any shared property, rather than one with literal types.
Believing `instanceof` can test against an interface, which has no runtime value.
Believing a user-defined type predicate is verified by the compiler, rather than trusted.
Believing an interface or type alias exists at runtime and can be inspected or passed as a value.
Believing two `type` aliases with the same name merge like interfaces, rather than being a duplicate identifier error.
Believing two structurally identical types are incompatible because they have different names.
Believing extra properties are always an error, rather than only for fresh object literals.
Believing `implements` copies members into the class, rather than only checking the class against the interface.
Believing generic type arguments exist at runtime and can be inspected or constructed with `new T()`.
Believing a generic parameter is inferred as the widest type rather than from the argument.
Believing `T extends U` in a constraint means T must be a class inheriting from U, rather than assignable to U.
Believing `Partial<T>` makes nested properties optional as well as the top level.
Believing `Readonly<T>` or `readonly` freezes the object at runtime.
Believing `Readonly<T>` makes nested object properties readonly.
Believing `Omit<T, K>` errors when K is not a key of T, rather than accepting any string key.
Believing indexing a `Record<string, T>` yields `T | undefined`, rather than T.
Believing a literal type stays narrow when assigned to a mutable property or `let`.
Believing `as const` freezes the value at runtime.
Believing template literal types validate string values at runtime.
Believing `any` and `unknown` behave the same, including allowing property access without a check.
Believing a value of type `unknown` can be assigned to any other type without narrowing.
Believing a variable of type `never` can hold a value at runtime.
Believing TypeScript `private` members are inaccessible at runtime, rather than only at compile time.
Believing a constructor parameter marked `public` or `private` also needs a separate field declaration.
Believing a string enum has a reverse mapping from value to name like a numeric enum.
Believing a `const enum` is always emitted as an object at runtime.
Believing type annotations are checked at runtime, so a wrong-typed value throws a TypeError.
Believing code with type errors never produces JavaScript output by default.
